summary: Overall the guide is scientifically careful and mostly correct. I re-derived or recomputed the main equations and all numerical examples: Poisson counts; the left-zero-vector projection and the 2D formulas; the Itô/Stratonovich conversion; the Fokker–Planck solution and the π²/3 wrapped limit; the S37 variance expansion; the Cauchy–Schwarz and residual-matrix bounds; the naive and ideal readout (coth); partial access; the two-time-scale left vector; the inverse filter and its static gain; the R² and χ algebra; filtered white versus filtered Brownian MSD; Kac–Rice; the inversion of mean field and gap length; the high-peak size laws; Rayleigh slopes; Euler-characteristic polynomials with box boundary factors; and the random-weight covariance. Each one checks out. Every independent check of a printed source equation that the guide labels is confirmed against the PDFs, and the guide keeps these separate from the official 2017 correction. Burak main Eq. 2 has no numerator square; S40 conflicts with S41 by a factor of 2; S71 has the wrong sign; S85 prints a positive rate-decay block; Eq. 6/S83 have the wrong inequality direction relative to the paper's own model; Mainali S18, S23 and S25 contain the stated errors; the counterexample showing equality does not force an exponential transfer rule holds. One reading needed a second look and is correct: Ben-Shushan Eq. 7 prints τ∓ with ±, so the guide's τ+ (slow) assignment and its phrase 'paired signs in Eq. 7' are right. No confirmed scientific error was found in the guide's own claims. The most important finding is reviewer-derived and concerns a modelling assumption shared by the paper and the guide (F01): the readout model treats observation noise as independent of the state increments. An observer reading the memory network's own spikes sees the same spike surplus that moves the state. Under the paper's linear synaptic model, the cue-state information then decays as e^{-t/τ}, giving asymptotic precision Jτ/2 rather than √(J/2D). The rest are qualifications of hardware descriptions, reasoning wording, citations I could not verify, and optional additions. Coverage limits: the open peer-review file text was not supplied and was not read; the MATLAB and Python code was not opened; several hardware and secondary sources were reached only through search snippets or not at all; no figure pixel audit was done.

findings.short_excerpt: In this approximation, these increments and errors are independent, zero-mean Gaussian variables. ... The derivations below are exact within this local Gaussian readout model.
findings.claim_or_gap: The observer reads the memory network's own spikes. The same spike surplus that moves θ (η_k = Σ v_i·ΔM_i) also produces the observation error (ε_k ∝ Σ (r_i'/r_i)·ΔM_i/J). At equality v_i = r_i'/(τJr_i), so η_k = (h/τ)ε_k: the two are perfectly correlated, not independent. A two-cell case can be checked exactly. In the linear mutual-inhibition network, r1 − r2 = θ/τ and dθ = dM1 − dM2, so the spike-difference observation is dY = (θ/τ)dt + dθ exactly. More generally, Eq. 7 gives s(t) = e^{−(t−T)/τ}s(T) + Σ_{spikes after T} e^{−(t−t_α)/τ}. Given the observed spikes, only s(T) is unknown, so ∂r_i(t)/∂θ(T) ≈ r_i'·e^{−(t−T)/τ}. The Poisson Fisher information about the cue state is then J∫₀^L e^{−2u/τ}du = (Jτ/2)(1 − e^{−2L/τ}). Its asymptotic variance is 2/(Jτ), not √(2D/J): at equality this is 4Dτ versus 2Dτ, and the approach time is τ/2 rather than 1/√(2DJ). The guide presents the paper's independent-noise model as describing readout of the memory network's spikes without naming the physical reason the approximation may fail.

source_evidence.what_it_supports: The observer 'has access to all spikes emitted by neurons in the memory network after the cue'; ξ_i and ζ_i are given as separate independent noises.
s is a linear filter of the neuron's own spikes, which is what makes the e^{−t/τ} decay of cue-state information exact given the observed spikes.
Linear two-cell model in which r1 − r2 = θ/τ, used for the exact check.

findings.strongest_retaining_reading: The guide calls this an 'approximation' and says the results are exact only 'within this local Gaussian readout model'. The partial-access section implicitly moves closer to independence as α decreases.
findings.why_it_is_still_a_problem: The reader's stated interest is the neural versus mathematical assumptions. The text never says the independence is physically violated when the observer receives the spikes that drive the memory. It then uses the model's asymptote √(2D/J) to judge the paper's Eq. 6 and to build the strict-inequality example. Those conclusions are valid inside the model. For full access with known dynamics, the different asymptote 2/(Jτ) gives a total ≤ 2D(T + 2τ), so Eq. 6 is still not universal but for a different reason. Readout 'within τ' remains true, and is even stronger.
findings.suggested_action: In sec:MEMORY-READOUT-SETUP, add one sentence: the model treats the state increments as unseen noise independent of the observed spikes, whereas the network's own spikes produce both. In a fold, state the full-access, known-dynamics result (precision Jτ/2 asymptotically) as a guide-derived check needing confirmation. Note that random partial access (small α) brings the observations closer to the independence assumption. Keep the Eq. 6 caution, but scope it to the paper's own readout model.
findings.confidence: medium (the algebra was checked on the exact linear two-cell case; the general case uses linearized rates and an observer that knows W, b, φ and τ)

findings.short_excerpt: If k0 means an absolute slope in Hz/degree, that printed expression has the wrong units for D.
findings.claim_or_gap: Eq. 1 is printed as a proportionality, which can carry a dimensional constant, so 'wrong units' alone is not decisive. The decisive point is the dependence on λ0 at fixed absolute slope. The derivation also inserts CV² into the 2012 Poisson information–diffusion relation. The 2022 integrator has saturating synapses (each spike adds 1/[τs(λt + λ)]), rectified rates, and a readout E_OI, so the 2012 bound applies only as a heuristic. My own rough check: the λ0-in-numerator conclusion survives for λ ≪ λt but the exponent changes for λ ≫ λt.

source_evidence.what_it_supports: Printed D ∝ CV² N⁻¹ λ0⁻¹ k0⁻² τs⁻², cited to Burak–Fiete.
Saturating synaptic response with λt = 60 Hz.

findings.strongest_retaining_reading: The guide labels the expression 'a scale', 'not an exact formula', and its own 'dimensional interpretation'.
findings.why_it_is_still_a_problem: A reader may take 'wrong units' as a proven printing error, and may assume the 2012 Poisson bound applies directly to the saturating sub-Poisson 2022 model.
findings.suggested_action: Rephrase: 'If k0 is an absolute slope, the 2012 Poisson relation implies D grows with λ0 at fixed slope; the printed λ0⁻¹ matches a fractional slope.' Add that synaptic saturation and sub-Poisson renewal statistics make this an order-of-magnitude guide.

findings.short_excerpt: Aitsam and colleagues ran a 768-neuron recurrent sheet on one chip, with signals from a physical event camera.
findings.claim_or_gap: The chip receives a host-computed, EMA-smoothed centroid injected as a fixed 2×2 cluster; it does not receive raw events. The on-chip network is deterministic integer-weight LIF with a period-two sustained orbit and no stochastic noise source, so 8 s persistence does not exercise noise-driven diffusion. Recurrence reduced jitter by 15% but increased mean error versus the target (5.65 vs 2.02 cells) and added about 115 ms of lag. Positions are also quantized to a 32×24 lattice, which is relevant to pinning (ch. 15).

source_evidence.what_it_supports: Host centroid and EMA; period-two orbit; ≤0.50-cell motion; error and lag trade-off.

findings.strongest_retaining_reading: The guide already says the 8 s is not a lifetime and that noise-controlled tests would be useful.
findings.why_it_is_still_a_problem: The connection to Burak–Fiete depends on whether noise is present and on what reaches the chip; both are omitted.
findings.suggested_action: Add one sentence: the input is a host-smoothed centroid; the deterministic on-chip network shows persistence but not diffusion; recurrence traded positional accuracy for stability.

findings.short_excerpt: m_{k+1} = α m_k + β z_k ... This model illustrates slow storage. It is not the full equations
findings.claim_or_gap: Sun's slow state is a frozen Legendre-memory (LMU) state-space realization (Ā = e^{AΔt}) that represents a sliding window of length θ, with spectral radius near 1. It is not a scalar leaky average, and it is neither a continuous attractor nor noise-driven.

source_evidence.what_it_supports: LMU A, B matrices; window θ; frozen discretized matrices.

findings.why_it_is_still_a_problem: The leaky illustration may lead readers to equate this engineered state with the neural memories of Part I.
findings.suggested_action: Add a clause naming the LMU sliding-window representation and stating that it stores a recent input history rather than a persistently held cue.

retained_strengths: Independent source checks are kept separate from the 2017 correction and labelled as algebra rather than author corrections; I confirmed each against the PDFs: missing Eq. 2 square, S40/S41, S71, S85, Eq. 6/S83, Mainali S18/S23/S25, and the equality-iff counterexample.
The left zero vector is explained through the tilted-decay example and Fig. 1A flow projection; this is the key bridge from neural mechanism to diffusion.

The χ versus R distinction is shown with a constructed numerical example (R = 0.17, χ = 0.82) and its calibration and independence assumptions; this prevents the common misreading of weak single-cell correlations.
The filtered white versus filtered Brownian MSD derivation (one-pole) explains why an intermediate log slope does not imply superdiffusion inside the circuit.
Careful separation of storage error from readout error, of naive from ideal readout, and of what Figs. 3/S2 compute (analytic) versus simulate.

The place-field chapters separate exact stationary results (Kac–Rice means, Rayleigh boundary slopes, EC) from high-threshold limits, quantify the 46% error at q = 1.1, and track fitted versus tested quantities per dataset.
The unit and convention checks throughout (D units, activation versus rate coordinates rescaled by 1/τ², σ versus filter width √2, MSD offset 2σm²) catch real pitfalls.

The hardware chapters consistently distinguish weight storage, neural state, and represented value; measured chip versus host versus post-layout simulation; and persistence versus measured lifetime. The reduced models are labelled guide-derived.
Explicit scope statements: the 2012 results are simulations, not animal data; the integrator is sufficient but not uniquely identified; the random-wiring interpretation is not measured.
